issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, sexual-violence comments as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile unless the index event also involved sexual assault or closely related content; nothing else in the profile supports that connection.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The appraisal of betrayal by a trusted person is difficult to fit with terrorism as the trauma type unless there was a clear interpersonal betrayal component; the rest of the selected items describe loss of control, helplessness, avoidance, dissociation, and substance use rather than interpersonal betrayal.

vignette:
Raj Patel is a 37-year-old clinical psychologist, married and South Asian, who sought treatment six months after surviving a terrorist attack at a downtown train station. He had been commuting home after a late patient session when a detonated pressure-cooker bomb plunged the platform into darkness, followed by a series of gunshots. Trapped under debris, he could not move or call out-utterly helpless-and the blackness was punctuated only by the pop of gunfire echoing off concrete. He was pulled out hours later, physically unharmed but profoundly shaken.

In the weeks that followed, Raj found himself raw in ways his clinical training could not repackage. Every evening, as dusk settled, his heart would pound; he would check locks repeatedly, certain that darkness invited danger. The mere sound of a car backfiring or a dropped book made him flinch and reach for his phone, ready to call 911. These triggers-especially moments when he felt something beyond his control, and the quiet dread of waking in the pitch-black bedroom-began dictating his life. When a trigger hit, the first thing Raj did was pour himself a glass of whiskey, sometimes two, to dull the jolt. He also started to mentally escape: during a difficult therapy session or even while having dinner with his wife, he would drift into a neutral fantasy of floating in a calm ocean, shutting out the present.

His clinical knowledge made the irony unbearable. He had taught patients about cognitive reappraisal, yet he could not stop the thought that the world was fundamentally dangerous-that another attack could happen at any moment. He became convinced that all his careful planning was pointless: bad things happened no matter what you did, and the person he had become-jumpy, withdrawn, dependent on alcohol and daydreams-felt unrecognisable. This sense of helplessness and alienation only deepened his reliance on his maladaptive strategies. On a particularly bad night, after waking in dark panic, he would drink more and then spend the next day avoiding any potential stressor: he cancelled all evening appointments, asked his supervisor to reassign trauma cases, and stopped driving near the station.

His avoidance, however, created new triggers. By shrinking his world, Raj ensured that any deviation-an unexpected phone call, a sudden change in schedule-felt catastrophic, reinforcing his belief that he could not control events. The drinking left him groggy, and on one occasion he woke disoriented at 3 a.m. in a dark room, the memory of the gunshots surging back. Similarly, his fantasy escapes, while soothing in the moment, left him feeling detached and unreal, which fed the appraisal that he no longer recognised himself.

Professionally, his reputation suffered. Colleagues noticed his reluctance to take on complex cases; one patient's report of a noisy construction site triggered a visible panic. His wife grew frustrated with his irritability and his insistence on sleeping with the bedside lamp on. Raj knew he needed help, but the very thought of admitting he had PTSD felt like confirmation that he was beyond repair-that even a psychologist could not fix himself.

What finally brought him to my office was a minor incident: a car door slamming in the parking lot sent him scrambling under his desk during a supervision session. His supervisor gently told him he was burned out and needed treatment. Raj came reluctantly, confiding that his greatest fear was that no therapy could undo the belief that the world was unsafe and that he had become a stranger to himself. He hoped, he said quietly, to at least stop the drinking and the escaping-because he was tired of feeling like a ghost in his own life.
